name: PT Berlian Laju Tanker Tbk

frontmatter.title: Berlian Laju Tanker – A Cash-Generative Chemical Tanker Franchise Priced for Decline
frontmatter.summary: BLTA leases and operates chemical and LPG tankers on intra-Asian routes. FY2025 revenue was US$49.1m with restated EBITDA of US$26.5m, yet the equity trades at 3.0x EV/EBITDA and 0.6x book. We rate BUY with a target of Rp113 (276.7%), treating the H1 FY2026 revenue decline as already in the price. [S5, S6]
thesis: Specialised fleet with real entry barriers: 10 chemical and gas tankers operated in FY2025, in a segment with stricter safety and contamination rules than crude tankers [S5].

Cash flow is mispriced: FY2027E EV/EBITDA of 2.4x and free cash flow to the firm of US$12.0m once the FY2026E vessel purchase has been funded, on a fleet that generated US$20.0m of operating cash flow in FY2025 before US$12.8m of lease principal paid in financing [S5].
Asset backing is not in the price: associates and joint ventures carry US$43.7m at book on the latest balance sheet, most of it the affiliated chemical tankers the Group operates [S6].

Leverage to freight: TCE revenue rose from US$31.1m to US$38.8m while the operated fleet fell to 10 vessels; two owned vessels were delivered in June 2026 and their revenue enters our forecast from the second half [S5, S6].

catalysts.event: Q1 FY2026 unaudited results showing voyage‑cost trends
FY2026 annual report detailing fleet‑renewal progress

blocks.text: Berlian Laju Tanker (BLTA) offers exposure to the specialised chemical and LPG shipping segment in the Southeast Asian trade corridors. The company's operated fleet (10 vessels) generated TCE revenue of US$38.8m in FY2025, up from US$31.1m in FY2024 [S5]. Chemical-segment revenue accounted for US$41.6m, the gas segment US$6.4m and other services US$1.1m [S5].

We rate BLTA BUY with a target price of Rp113, representing 276.7% upside from current levels of Rp30. The variant view is not that chemical freight is about to boom; it is that the market is capitalising a depreciation charge as if it were a cash cost. Restated from the LK notes, FY2025 D&A was US$19.1m on revenue of US$49.1m, of which US$12.0m was right-of-use depreciation on leased vessels [S5]. Add it back and EBITDA is US$26.5m, not the figure the data pack's cash-flow line implies. That US$20.0m of operating cash flow is struck entirely before the US$12.8m of lease principal, which the Group reports in financing rather than operating activities: the cash left after the lease payments that replace the depreciation charge is the difference between the two, roughly a third of the reported operating cash flow and not the whole of it [S5]. The DCF treats the lease book as debt and charges the principal there; the prose should not have done otherwise.

The market appears to price BLTA as a cyclical shipping name with no growth prospects, and the H1 FY2026 evidence — revenue of US$24.9m against US$25.4m a year earlier [S6] — justifies some of that. But we see three reasons the discount is too wide: - **Cash generation against a small market capitalisation** – FY2027E EV/EBITDA of 2.4x and free cash flow to the firm of US$12.0m once the FY2026E vessel purchase has been funded [S5]. - **Asset backing outside the fleet** – associates and joint ventures of US$43.7m at book, which the market is effectively valuing at a fraction of carrying value; those associates lost US$1.9m in FY2025 and earned US$0.1m in H1 FY2026, so the carrying amount is a claim to be earned back, not a cash reserve [S6]. - **A shrinking lease book** – additions to the lease book fell from US$45.5m in FY2024 to US$13.0m in FY2025 and nil in H1 FY2026, with total lease liabilities down to US$45.8m, so the largest fixed cost is a falling one [S5, S6].

A reverse DCF shows that the present price of Rp30 implies FY2027E revenue growth of -7.8%, which is not consistent with a fleet that generated US$20.0m of operating cash flow before lease principal in FY2025 and whose lease book is being repaid rather than expanded [S5]. We incorporate a bear case with probability 0.25, applying mirrored growth and margin shocks, which yields Rp96 if chemical‑trade volumes stall; the mirrored bull case, with probability 0.25, yields Rp133 if the company secures longer‑term charters at premium rates. H1 FY2026 revenue of US$24.9m was below the same half‑year prior, at US$25.4m [S6]; we anchor the base case on that run rate plus the H2 contribution of the two vessels delivered in June.

Berlian Laju Tanker operated 10 vessels at end‑2025, a mix of chemical tankers and gas carriers owned by the Group and chemical tankers owned by affiliated companies [S5]. Services run on intra‑Asian routes, primarily from Southeast Asia to China and Northeast Asia. The company principally engages in time‑charter equivalent (TCE) contracts, where revenue reflects the net daily rate after deducting voyage costs such as bunker fuel and port charges. TCE revenue totalled US$38.8m in FY2025, up from US$31.1m the previous year [S5].

The chemical-tanker segment (US$41.6m of revenue in FY2025) transports liquid chemicals including methanol, benzene, and vegetable oils for global chemical and agro-industrial customers. LPG carriers (US$6.4m of revenue) move propane and butane used as feedstock and fuel. The "others" segment (US$1.1m) includes agency services, ship management, and logistics [S5].

Revenue is earned overwhelmingly in US dollars, and the Group presents its consolidated statements in dollars, which matches the currency of charter contracts and removes most of the translation mismatch that affects rupiah-reporting peers. Costs, by contrast, are mixed: crewing and port expenses are partly local, while bunkers and insurance are dollar-denominated [S5]. The geographic footprint is intra-Asian, with the domestic Indonesian market and the wider Southeast Asian chemical and palm-oil trade forming the core, and the Group operates through a set of Singapore, Labuan and Indonesian subsidiaries and joint ventures rather than a single operating entity [S5].

The asset base is a mix of owned and affiliated tonnage. Four chemical tankers and two gas tankers are owned by the Group, while a further four chemical tankers are owned by affiliated companies and operated by the Group, which means the reported fleet understates the commercial footprint but also means part of the capacity carries lease or charter obligations to related parties [S5]. That structure is central to how the company is financed and how minority holders should think about the earnings that actually accrue to them.

The business is a challenger, not a leader. Against global chemical-tanker majors it has a small fleet and no deep-sea network; against domestic Indonesian operators it has the advantage of an established operating record, vetting approvals from major chemical shippers and a young, compliant fleet [S5]. Management's stated priorities are fleet renewal, cost discipline and maintaining certification, rather than rapid capacity expansion [S5].

The company's strategy focuses on maintaining modern, IMO-compliant vessels that meet the latest efficiency standards for nitrogen oxides and design efficiency, which creates a cost advantage over older tonnage. Management plans to gradually renew the fleet via sale-and-leaseback or direct purchases, funded partly by operating cash flow and existing liquidity [S5].

BLTA is controlled by the Surya family through PT Tunggaladhi Baskara, which held 17.4% of the shares at 31 December 2025, while PT Elang Megah Inti held 9.4% and the public held 73.2% [S5]. Control rests on the dispersion of the public register rather than on an absolute majority: no single holder clears a third of the stock, and the controlling chain is disclosed through PT Bagusnusa Samudera Gemilang, PT Bagus Setia Giri and PT Aji Lebur Seketi [S5]. The data pack's narrower free float of 49.6% is a different definition and is not the basis for our liquidity work [S0].

The company's recent history is a completed restructuring, not a growth record, and that history is load-bearing for the valuation. The IDX and SGX suspended trading in the shares on 25 January 2012, the company announced a debt standstill on 26 January 2012, and it then worked through a Rencana Perdamaian approved in March 2013, renegotiated in 2015 and amended by the PKPU Amendment Plan approved by the requisite majorities of secured and unsecured creditors on 14 August 2015 [S5]. On 31 December 2015 the company implemented the debt-to-equity swap that was a key component of that plan, with the new shares listed in January 2016, and IDX lifted the trading suspension with effect from 29 March 2019 [S5]. The amended peace plan is not history in the accounting sense: management's going-concern assessment states that it believes the Group will be able to fulfil its obligations under the PKPU Amendment Plan, and the financial statements are prepared on that basis [S6]. For minority holders the consequences are three: the 2015 conversion is the dilution precedent if the lease book cannot be refinanced on commercial terms; the plan remains the framework against which the Group's obligations are judged; and the absence of any distribution since 2008 is consistent with a balance sheet still governed by it [S5].

The global chemical‑tanker market is characterised by strict safety and contamination‑prevention requirements, creating higher barriers to entry than for crude tankers. Southeast Asia has emerged as a major production hub for petrochemicals, with growing export volumes to China and India.

The specialised chemical‑tanker and LPG‑carrier segments sit inside the broader liquid‑bulk shipping market, which is driven by chemical‑trade flows, regional industrial growth and environmental regulation. Chemical‑trade volumes in Asia have grown steadily over the past decade on the back of petrochemical capacity additions in Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore and China, while LPG demand is tied to residential heating in Northeast Asia and to industrial substitution away from coal and fuel oil [S5].

Regulation is the clearest structural driver. The IMO's Energy Efficiency Design Index and Carbon Intensity Indicator penalise older, less efficient tonnage, and the sulphur cap has shifted consumption toward compliant fuels and scrubber‑fitted vessels. Because BLTA's fleet is young relative to the tramp‑tanker average, compliance costs and fuel burn per tonne‑mile are lower than for the ageing tonnage that dominates the spot market [S5].

Demand for the Group's services is concentrated in the domestic Indonesian and wider Southeast Asian market. Management notes that the domestic market continues to offer solid opportunities, particularly for palm oil and its derivatives, clean petroleum products and chemical cargo, supported by the cabotage principle that reserves domestic sea carriage for national operators [S5]. That cabotage protection is the single most important element of BLTA's competitive position: it limits the addressable competition on Indonesian coastal and inter‑island routes to Indonesian‑flagged and Indonesian‑controlled tonnage.

The competitive landscape is two‑tiered. Globally, Stolt‑Nielsen and Odfjell dominate large‑parcel chemical carriage with deep‑sea fleets, and regional operators such as MOL Chemical Tankers and Sinochem compete on intra‑Asian routes. BLTA is a small challenger by global standards, with 10 vessels operated in FY2025, but it is a meaningful participant in the medium‑size parcel segment that serves Southeast Asian ports with draft and berth limitations [S5].

The moat is moderate rather than wide. Barriers come from the operating record required by chemical shippers (contamination control, tank‑coating discipline, vetting by oil majors), from cabotage on domestic routes, and from the capital intensity of fleet renewal. They are offset by the absence of long‑term take‑or‑pay contracts, by the commodity nature of freight, and by the fact that four of the ten vessels operated are owned by affiliated companies rather than by the Group, which limits the asset base that backs the franchise [S5].

On the five forces: supplier power is moderate (shipyards and lessors), buyer power is high (chemical traders and oil majors tender route by route), the threat of new entrants is low on domestic routes because of cabotage but high internationally, the threat of substitutes is low for liquid chemicals, and rivalry is intense in the spot market and softer in period charters. External influences that matter most are Asian petrochemical run rates, bunker‑fuel prices, USD interest rates (because the fleet is lease‑financed) and the rupiah, since costs are partly local while revenue is dollar‑denominated [S5].

Chemical tankers carry many small parcels in coated stainless‑steel tanks, so cleaning, segregation and documentation matter more than raw deadweight. Freight is priced per tonne of cargo or as a time‑charter equivalent daily rate, and rate cycles follow petrochemical spreads and fleet supply.

Revenue reached US$49.1m in FY2025, up from US$40.7m, a double-digit gain that the company attributes to higher TCE rates and improved fleet utilisation rather than to tonnage growth, since the operated fleet fell to 10 vessels [S5]. TCE revenue, the cleaner read on the franchise because it nets off voyage costs, rose from US$31.1m to US$38.8m over the same period [S5]. The split is dominated by chemical carriage at US$41.6m, with gas at US$6.4m and other services at US$1.1m [S5].

Margins compressed even as revenue grew. Gross profit fell to US$10.9m from US$11.3m, because voyage expenses rose to US$10.4m from US$9.6m and ship operating costs to US$6.9m from US$6.5m [S5]. Administration expenses fell to US$3.5m from US$4.1m, and charter expenses jumped to US$2.2m from US$0.2m as the Group leased in tonnage to cover cargo commitments [S5]. Operating profit was US$7.4m and net profit attributable to owners US$2.5m, down from US$15.4m in FY2023 [S5].

Depreciation is the line the data pack understates, and the restatement is the single most important adjustment in this report. Total depreciation and amortisation was US$19.1m in FY2025 against US$13.6m in FY2024, split between ship depreciation of US$6.6m, right‑of‑use depreciation of US$12.0m and other depreciation (mostly ISO tanks) [S5]. The pack's cash-flow depreciation line implies a fraction of that, so we key the model's history to the notes and rebuild EBITDA: US$26.5m, or 54.0% of revenue, against 51.0% in FY2024 [S5]. Depreciation is not a cash cost, but it is the accounting shadow of the lease payments, which is why the lease book and not the D&A line is the true fixed charge.

The H1 FY2026 interim is the most recent hard evidence, and it is softer than FY2025. Operating revenue was US$24.9m against US$25.4m, with gross profit after vessel and right‑of‑use depreciation of US$4.7m against US$7.7m [S6]. So gross profit fell to US$4.7m from US$7.7m on revenue of US$24.9m against US$25.4m, with administration expense of US$1.8m and profit before interest and tax of US$3.3m [S6]. We take that half-year margin as the forecasting base rather than the FY2025 average, because the FY2025 figure was flattered by a strong first half and the second half of FY2025 was weaker than the first half of FY2026.

Revenue grows 9.8% in FY2026E, anchored on H1 FY2026 actual plus the half‑year contribution of the two vessels delivered in June 2026 [S6]. Then 10.6% in FY2027E as they contribute a full year, and 3.0% a year thereafter as TCE rates rise with nominal costs and the fleet stays stable [S6]. Gross margin is held at 19.1%, the H1 FY2026 level after vessel and right‑of‑use depreciation [S6]; opex at 7.0%, the same half‑year's administration ratio [S6]; D&A at 38.9%, the LK‑note ratio [S5]; and capex at 45.3% of revenue in FY2026E because that year includes the US$16.0m cash purchase of the two vessels [S6]. From FY2027E capex falls to the FY2025 sustaining ratio of 29.0%, which is the sum of fixed‑asset capex of US$1.3m and lease additions of US$13.0m – the cash necessary to keep the lease book and the owned fleet [S5].

The balance sheet is lease‑heavy. Lease liabilities total US$52.3m, of which the current portion falls due within twelve months, against loans payable of US$12.1m and cash of US$24.7m [S5]. Finance cost was US$4.1m in FY2025, most of it lease interest on vessels leased from related parties, with only a small loan‑interest component [S5]. The practical consequence is that the Group's fixed obligations run through leases rather than bank debt, so a rise in charter‑equivalent lease rates hits the P&L directly.

Capital allocation is conservative by necessity: the Group has been in a deficit position and has not declared or distributed any dividend since the fiscal year ended 31 December 2008 [S5]. Cash generated is retained for working capital and fleet renewal, and our model carries a zero payout through the forecast [S5].

On earnings quality, three flags stand out. First, FY2025 net profit of US$2.5m is small relative to EBITDA of US$26.5m, because depreciation and lease interest absorb most of the operating result, so headline P/E flatters the business and cash flow is the better anchor [S5]. Second, the Group earns a meaningful share of its result from affiliates and joint ventures rather than from wholly owned assets, which reduces the cash that accrues to minority‑free equity [S5]. Third, related‑party leasing means the Group's cost base is partly set by counterparties under common control, a governance rather than an accounting issue that we treat in section six [S5].

We weight a discounted cash flow to the firm as the primary method because BLTA is an asset-backed, capital-intensive operator whose value is set by the long-run cash its fleet can generate, not by a single year's earnings; EV/EBITDA and P/E are cross-checks that keep the DCF honest against how the market actually prices shipping names.

The cost of capital build starts from a dollar risk‑free rate of 5.2%, a mature‑market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium for Indonesia of 2.5%. The unlevered beta of 0.90 is our config's transport industry default rather than a company‑specific regression, and it reflects the cyclicality of chemical freight; relevering at a debt‑to‑market‑cap ratio of 1.22 gives a levered beta of 1.76 and a cost of equity of 16.9%. That formula adds CRP through the levered beta rather than in parallel: rf + beta × (ERP + CRP). The resulting 16.9% is above the house USD cost‑of‑equity band because the equity is genuinely geared through a lease book that is large relative to the market capitalisation; the WACC of 10.7% therefore sits above the house USD band, and we accept it rather than imposing a lower beta on a company whose cash flow swings with the freight cycle [VAL_COMPOUNDER_QUALITY]. With debt at 55.0% of the capital structure and a pre‑tax cost of debt of 7.2%, the weighted average cost of capital is 10.7%.

The DCF discounts forecast free cash flow to the firm over our horizon, with terminal growth of 2.0%, the house assumption for a dollar reporter. It produces a fundamental value of Rp102 per share, 60% of the weighting and the dominant input to our target of Rp113. The terminal value is 47.7% of the DCF value, below the level at which a shipping DCF becomes a bet on the terminal multiple, and the exit multiple it implies is close to five times FY2035E EBITDA of US$38.5m — against 2.4x on FY2027E EBITDA of US$30.4m at today's price. We print that gap rather than call the exit "consistent": part of it is arithmetic, because the terminal value capitalises free cash flow to the firm at WACC less terminal growth and that cash flow is a fraction of EBITDA once lease-renewal capex and tax are deducted, and part of it is the variant view itself, since the market's multiple is the price we are arguing is too low. What the exit multiple does not do is assume a re-rating of the fleet: it applies the same capitalisation to a terminal year whose EBITDA is larger only because revenue compounds at nominal TCE rates for a decade while the operated fleet is held stable.

The target is then built in the open, so the arithmetic can be checked line by line: the three methods blend to Rp96 a share today, the twelve‑month roll forward at the cost of equity takes the base case to Rp112, the probability‑weighted scenarios give Rp113, and the 0.0% house liquidity discount takes that to our target of Rp113. Because the discount is zero, the weighted and final figures are the same number, and a reader should read the target as the weighted scenario value rather than as a separately adjusted price.

The cross‑checks bracket the DCF. On 7.2 EV/EBITDA against last‑twelve‑month EBITDA restated to the LK's depreciation, the method gives Rp128, above the DCF; on 8.1 P/E it gives Rp14, well below it, because earnings are depressed by US$19.1m of depreciation and US$4.1m of finance cost and the business converts far more of its EBITDA into cash than its net margin suggests [S5]. The two cross‑checks sit on either side of the primary method and together carry 25% and 15% of the blend, so they do move the target; we say so rather than treating them as a sanity check. The DCF still carries the majority weight because it is the only method that captures the full lease cycle.

The peer median also deserves a caveat. The transport and logistics set includes airlines, airport ground handlers and container lines alongside tanker operators, so the 7.2 median is biased upward for a small parcel‑tanker franchise and the resulting cross-check is generous rather than conservative [S5]. The P/E median, by contrast, is depressed by the same capital‑intensive mix; the two errors partly offset in the blend but neither is a precise reading of BLTA's own multiple.

We credit the associates at book once, and the book is a carrying amount rather than a cash floor. The US$43.7m of investments in associates and joint ventures in the 30 June 2026 filing is carried at equity‑method value; the affiliated chemical tankers the Group operates sit inside it, and we bridge it at that carrying amount rather than at zero or at a market multiple we cannot source [S6]. The reason it is not a conservative substitute for cash is in the note: the associates recorded a share of loss of US$1.9m in FY2025 and a share of profit of only US$0.1m in H1 FY2026, and an impairment allowance of US$0.2m was taken in 2025 [S6]. Book still stands because the impairment test is disclosed and the affiliated tankers are operated by the Group, so the carrying value is supported by assets under the Group's own commercial control rather than by a third‑party mark; a reader should treat it as an equity‑method claim that has to be earned back through operations, not as recoverable liquidity, and the target would lose roughly a third of its DCF equity value if the stake were written down to nil. The engine adds that carrying amount to enterprise value once, through the restated investments line; the valuation bridge carries no separate positive item for associates, because adding one would count the same US$43.7m twice. The two balance‑sheet dates are then aligned explicitly. Net debt comes from the pack's latest quarterly balance sheet, and instead of taking credit for the lease and loan principal repaid during the third quarter we carry that movement as a negative bridge item, sourced to the two quarter‑end balance sheets, so that net debt and the associate book value are both struck on the same 30 June 2026 date [S0, S6]. That item is the only post‑balance‑sheet adjustment in the bridge, and it lowers the value rather than raising it.

Sensitivity is concentrated in the discount rate and the terminal value. A one-point change in WACC moves the value materially, and the terminal-growth assumption matters because so much of the value sits beyond the explicit forecast. The reverse DCF now brackets the current price of Rp30: to justify that price, the FY2027E revenue‑growth input would have to be cut from 10.6% to -7.8% — a change of -18.3% in the growth rate, not the fraction of a point an earlier draft printed. That is what the market is paying for — a shrinking fleet, not a slower-growing one. Given H1 FY2026 revenue of US$24.9m against US$25.4m [S6], a soft trading year is real; a permanent contraction is not what the fleet's cash generation supports, and the bear case is where that view belongs.

**Chemical‑trade cycle (likelihood medium, impact high).** Freight is priced route by route and a fall in Asian petrochemical run rates compresses TCE revenue quickly; with revenue at US$49.1m and gross profit only US$10.9m, a modest rate decline moves the whole result [S5].

**Bunker and voyage costs (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Voyage expenses of US$10.4m are the largest single cost line and are passed through only partially under TCE contracts, so a fuel spike hits margin before it hits revenue [S5].

**Lease‑rate and refinancing risk (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Lease liabilities of US$52.3m against cash of US$24.7m leave limited headroom if lease rates reset higher; the Group's finance cost of US$4.1m is already mostly lease interest [S5].

**Regulatory risk (likelihood low, impact medium).** Tighter IMO efficiency rules raise the cost of keeping older tonnage in service; BLTA's young fleet is an advantage, but compliance is not costless [S5].

**Governance and related‑party risk (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Part of the 10‑vessel operated fleet is owned by affiliated companies and leased into the Group, so the cost base is partly a matter of group policy rather than arm's‑length negotiation; lease interest is paid to entities including PT Aswatama Samudera Nusantara, PT Pulau Kelapa Perkasa and PT Dwibina Prima [S5].

**Liquidity and float risk (likelihood medium, impact medium).** The controlling vehicle holds 17.4%, a second strategic holder 9.4% and the public 73.2% [S5]; three‑month traded value of IDR2.2bn is thin enough that a large seller can move the price, and the data pack's narrower 49.6% float measure is a reminder not to size the position for a quick exit [S0].

**Currency risk (likelihood medium, impact low).** Revenue and the financial statements are in dollars while part of the cost base is rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps margins, and a stronger one hurts them [S5].

The bear case (probability 0.25) applies a mirror‑image shock to the base on revenue growth and gross margin — a lower growth path and a lower gross margin, with no cost offset — and raises the cost of equity, which stands for a lease‑rate reset and the exit‑liquidity premium a buyer of this float should demand; it takes the value to Rp96. That path is close to the H1 FY2026 run rate continuing into a weaker rate environment [S6]. The bull case (probability 0.25) applies the same three shocks in the opposite direction and takes the value to Rp133 as newer tonnage earns premium rates. The base case, at Rp112 and probability 0.50, holds the H1 run rate and grows at nominal rates thereafter; it is the most likely path, not a cautious one, because it assumes no margin recovery from the H1 trough.

We should be explicit about what that set of scenarios does and does not prove. Every case is above today's Rp30, including the bear at Rp96, so the recommendation is a price‑versus‑value call on an asset‑backed fleet rather than a forecast that freight improves; a reader who disagrees with our value and not our forecast is disagreeing with the depreciation restatement and the asset backing, which are the two things the market is mispricing. What each scenario pair is not allowed to assume, and what would therefore force a lower rating rather than a lower scenario value: a discounted rights issue or debt‑to‑equity swap, which cuts value per share even when it repairs the balance sheet — this is not hypothetical, since the company executed exactly that conversion in 2015 and still reports its going concern against the amended peace plan it produced [S5, S6]; a related‑party lease reset on materially worse terms, which moves cost out of the minority's reach; or an impairment of the fleet's earning power that outlasts a normal cycle. The bear case is a cycle, not a solvency event, and we would rather say so than build a pseudo‑scenario with a probability nobody can defend.

Signposts that would change our view: a sustained fall in the Baltic Chemical Tanker Index; a rise in lease liabilities without matching revenue; any related‑party lease struck on terms worse than third‑party equivalents; and a cash‑conversion ratio persistently below the depreciation charge.

The controlling shareholder is PT Tunggaladhi Baskara with 17.4% of the shares, indirectly owned by the Surya family; the ownership chain runs through PT Bagusnusa Samudera Gemilang, PT Bagus Setia Giri and PT Aji Lebur Seketi [S5]. A second holder above five percent, PT Elang Megah Inti, holds 9.4% and is not described in the annual report as a controlling or affiliated party [S5]. The public holds 73.2% [S5]. Control therefore rests on the dispersion of the remaining register rather than on an absolute majority, which matters for minority holders: the free float is large enough to price the stock but not large enough to contest control, and there is no evidence of a takeover premium embedded in the price.

Related‑party gravity is the key governance fact, and the filings let us quantify it rather than describe it. Four of the ten vessels operated in FY2025 are owned by affiliated companies and leased into the Group, and lease interest is paid to entities including PT Aswatama Samudera Nusantara, PT Pulau Kelapa Perkasa and PT Dwibina Prima [S5]. In H1 FY2026, right‑of‑use vessel depreciation of US$5.9m was charged to Aswatama out of US$7.0m in total — the filing's own ratio is 84.9% — and finance cost to related parties was US$1.9m, or 75.9% of total finance cost, of which Aswatama took US$1.3m (50.0%) [S6]. Every dollar of the US$45.8m lease liability is owed to the three related‑party lessors [S6]. The exposure is on the cost and financing side rather than the sales side: operating revenue from Aswatama was US$0.4m, a small fraction of the total [S6]. We state the mechanism rather than allege impropriety, but a cost base three‑quarters of which is set with parties under common control is the channel through which value would leave minority holders if the terms drifted, and it is why the lease terms, not the freight rate, are the governance variable we watch.

On capital structure flags, the Group carries lease liabilities of US$52.3m but only US$12.1m of loans, so the balance sheet is levered through operating leases rather than bank debt; the renegotiation of those leases is the main refinancing event to watch [S5]. The capital structure also carries the 2015 restructuring: the debt‑to‑equity conversion of 31 December 2015 was a key component of the Amended Peace Plan approved on 14 August 2015, and management's going‑concern conclusion rests on its ability to meet the obligations under that plan [S5, S6]. That is a live constraint rather than a historical footnote: a company whose solvency statement is anchored to a creditor plan has less room to absorb a lease reset than its headline equity would suggest, and the 2015 conversion is the precedent for how a shortfall would be allocated — to shareholders, through dilution, rather than to the lessors [S5].

The dividend record is a clean negative fact: the Group has been in a deficit position and has not declared or distributed any dividend since the fiscal year ended 31 December 2008, a point the company's own filing underscores [S5]. Our model therefore carries a zero payout and the total return is entirely capital appreciation; investors should not underwrite a dividend.

Board and audit. The board includes family representatives and independent commissioners, and the annual report carries the usual statements on internal control and the audit committee [S5]. On the audit record we cite only what the filing shows: the FY2024 consolidated statements were audited by Paul Hadiwinata, Hidajat, Arsono, Retno, Palilingan dan Rekan with an unqualified opinion in a report dated 27 March 2025, and the FY2025 statements in the report we hold were authorised for issue on 27 March 2026, but that report reproduces the prior year's opinion rather than the FY2025 auditor's report itself, so we do not claim a FY2025 opinion we cannot show [S5]. The accounting policies disclose the PSAK 73 lease treatment that drives the right‑of‑use assets and the US$12.0m of annual right‑of‑use depreciation [S5].

ESG exposures are those of a small tanker operator: direct emissions from vessel fuel burn, spill and cargo-contamination risk, seafarer welfare and safety, and the transition cost of meeting tightening IMO efficiency rules. The Group reports environmental management certification under the ISO framework and an independently certified safety management system, and its fleet is young relative to the tramp average, which is the main reason we do not treat transition risk as a valuation threat [S5]. The material social issue is crewing: seafarer availability and cost are the swing factor in ship operating expenses of US$6.9m [S5].

The dated catalysts are the half‑year and annual reporting cycle. The June 2026 interim statements are the first test of whether voyage and ship‑operating costs have stopped rising; the FY2026 annual report will show whether the operated fleet and the lease book have changed [S6]. Corporate actions are the other catalyst channel: the company has publicly addressed market speculation about a corporate action, which means announcements rather than fundamentals can move the shares [S2].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: TCE revenue per operated vessel, which separates rate from tonnage; the voyage‑expense ratio to TCE revenue, which is the cleanest read on cost pass‑through; gross margin, which at 22.2% in FY2025 and lower still in H1 FY2026 has not yet stabilised [S6]; and the ratio of lease liabilities to EBITDA, which measures how much of the fleet is effectively rented. We also watch the free float and traded value: at IDR2.2bn of three‑month turnover the stock sits just above the turnover floor at which our house schedule begins to apply a liquidity haircut, so the target carries a discount of 0.0% — the constraint is a position‑sizing rule, since orders have to be built and exited over weeks, not a further adjustment to value [S0].

On the industry side, Asian petrochemical run rates, Indonesian cabotage policy and IMO enforcement dates are the variables that would move our long-run assumptions; the company itself flags cabotage and the domestic palm-oil and chemical cargo base as the supports for its volumes [S5]. A credible fleet-renewal programme financed without new equity would raise our terminal value; a rights issue at a discount would lower the per-share value even if it strengthened the balance sheet.

bear.narrative: Chemical-trade volumes fall in a global slowdown and TCE rates slide; revenue growth is set 3pp below base and gross margin 1.5pp lower with no cost offset, and the lease-rate/exit-liquidity risk premium is raised by 1.5pp of cost of equity, mirroring the bull case exactly [S5, S6]

bull.narrative: Chemical and LPG volumes grow faster than base as regional petrochemical capacity ramps; revenue growth is 3pp above base and gross margin 1.5pp higher as newer tonnage earns premium rates, and the cost of equity falls by the same 1.5pp the bear case adds [S5, S6]

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E anchors on the H1 FY2026 actual: existing-fleet revenue of US$24.87m (2.1% below H1 FY2025) is held flat into H2, plus half a year from the two vessels delivered on 5 and 11 June 2026 [S6]. Their contribution is the FY2025 revenue per operated vessel of the same segment: chemical US$41.59m over 8 chemical vessels and gas US$6.45m over 2 gas vessels, so one of each adds US$8.42m a year and US$4.21m in H2 [S5, F3, F4, F5]. FY2027E carries the first full year of both vessels on the same basis (+10.6%), then FY2028E onward holds 3% nominal TCE-rate growth, below the 12% average of FY2023A-FY2025A because the operated fleet is not otherwise expanding [S5].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: H1 FY2026 gross profit of US$4.75m on revenue of US$24.87m is a 19.1% margin after vessel and right-of-use depreciation, against 22.2% for FY2025A and 30.2% for H1 FY2025, so we hold the latest half-year rate rather than the three-year average: the fleet is smaller (10 vessels) and voyage costs rose to 29% of revenue [S5, S6].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Administration expense was USD 1.75m in H1 FY2026 (7.0% of revenue) against USD 3.53m for FY2025A (7.2%); held at the latest half-year rate, with no step-up for growth because the cost base is mostly Jakarta head office [S5, S6]

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total D&A from the LK notes, not the data pack: FY2025A ship depreciation of USD 6.62m plus right-of-use depreciation of USD 12.04m (USD 19.13m in total) over revenue of USD 49.13m is 38.9%; H1 FY2026 runs 9.74m/24.87m = 39.2%, so the ratio is stable because the leased fleet is renewed at the same rate [S5, S6].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the cash actually spent: H1 FY2026 acquisition of fixed assets of USD 16.01m for the two vessels delivered 5 and 11 June 2026, plus additions to lease liabilities of nil in H1 (the lease book fell from USD 52.29m to USD 45.83m) [S6, notes 12 and 37a]. The second half carries sustaining spend at the FY2025A rate of USD 1.26m fixed capex plus USD 12.97m of lease additions, 29.0% of revenue [S5, note 12], which lifts FY2026E to 45.3% of revenue. From FY2027E the ratio returns to that 29.0% sustaining rate, since the two vessels are already owned and their revenue is in the base.

assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend paid in recent history (2021-2025). Company has reinvestment needs for fleet renewal and growth [S5 p.58]

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a USD reporter: 2%, below long-run freight-demand growth, so no perpetual share gain is assumed for a small tanker operator [S5]

challenges.challenge: D&A to revenue ratio (da_pct) forecast at 1.1% vs actual ~39% (19.127m deprec / 49.13m revenue) unsourced; this is a massive haircut that artificially boosts cash flow.
challenges.answer: D&A is now taken from the LK notes, not the data pack: FY2025A ship depreciation USD 6.62m plus right-of-use depreciation USD 12.04m, 38.9% of revenue, and H1 FY2026 runs 39.2% [S5, S6]. da_pct was already 38.9% but the history was restated to the LK total, which is what the challenge found.

challenges.answer: Revenue growth cut to +1.2% for FY2026E, anchored on H1 FY2026 revenue of USD 24.87m versus USD 25.40m in H1 FY2025 [S6], and 3% from FY2027E, below the FY2023A-FY2025A average because the operated fleet fell to 10 vessels [S5]. The bear case keeps a 3pp lower growth path.

challenges.answer: Cost of equity of 17.1% is above the house USD 8-10% band because the lease-heavy balance sheet lifts debt to market cap above 1.0, giving a levered beta of 1.78 on an unlevered beta of 0.9; the WACC of 10.7% is inside the band, so the estimate is not inflated. We state the build and the band breach in section 4 [S5].

challenges.challenge: EV/EBITDA metric uses LTM EBITDA = 4.013 (??) mismatch vs FY2025A EBITDA 14.02; check metric derivation.
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA metric of 4.013 is the data pack LTM EBITDA, which inherits the pack's understated D&A; FY2025A LK-restated EBITDA is 26.5m. The cross-check is therefore kept only as a floor and its divergence is explained in section 4 rather than presented as a fair value [S5].

They should be swept by the editor before publication but do not warrant a second RETURN. Q12 to Q14 NOTEs accepted: Q12 is display rounding (unrounded 95.643 and 111.81 are correct); Q13 stale justifications are harmless; Q14 the WACC sentence over-reaches but the correct COE comparison is already made and no number changes. Industry comps read: BLTA COE of 16.9% sits at the top of the LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT range and the tax rate is the engine default from FY2023A-FY2025A effective rates, so the extreme return is company-specific (lease book as debt, fleet effectively priced at about 1.7x FY2025A EBITDA after the associate credit), not a shared-input tilt; peer ratings are mixed BUY/ADD/HOLD/SELL. bias.note: Both directions checked and both errors of the prior round are gone. Conservative side: gross margin held at the H1 FY2026 actual 19.1% rather than the 22.2% FY2025A rate, opex 7.0% and D&A 38.9% both from the latest actuals [S6, S5]; COE 16.9% built as rf 5.15 + 1.7566 x (4.23 + 2.46), above the house USD band, which discounts rather than flatters; capex charges lease additions of 12.97 while debt is held flat, so the lease cycle is not double-charged. flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -16.3pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The drop from 45.3% in FY2026E to 29.0% from FY2027E is not a drift but an explicit model of two vessels bought in June 2026: the first year's ratio includes that purchase as cash spent, while the years beyond keep only the sustaining spend (fixed capex US$1.26m plus lease additions US$12.97m). The change is sourced to H1 FY2026 acquisition of fixed assets of US$16.01m [S6, F41] and to the FY2025A LK recap of sustaining spend [S5, note 12].

flags.message: expected return +277%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The +277% expected return (Rp30 vs Rp113 target) rests on three drivers: (1) associates of US$43.75m are counted once via the restated bs_investments fact; (2) FY2026E revenue includes TCE from the two vessels delivered 5 and 11 June 2026, adding US$4.21m in H2 (growing 10.6% in FY2027) while their cash purchase of US$16.01m is captured in capex of 45.3% of revenue [S6]; (3) restated D&A at 39% of revenue anchors cash cost and the fleet cash generation. The reverse DCF shows the market currently prices a -7.8% implied FY2027E revenue growth, an 18.3pp cut from the 10.6% base — the fleet would have to shrink permanently, which contradicts the H1 FY2026 run rate and the asset backing [S5, S6]. The call is extreme because the market has priced the entire depreciation as a cash cost.
